<reason>Both sides were sharp and both suffered clipping, so this came down to who resolved the clash more cleanly. PRO's thesis ("a hidden increase should be visible") is intuitively strong and its dilemma (inattention kills your unit-price fix too) was the best pressure of the debate. But CON answered it directly and coherently (attention is scarce, not zero; one number at the point of decision vs. a second competing historical sticker), then did the more disciplined comparative work: tracking how PRO's "line of code" grew into a "substantially similar" adjudication across SKUs, pressing the warning-fatigue arithmetic that PRO never really answered beyond "honest design," and offering a consistent decision rule (information that improves the purchase vs. information that provokes a reaction). PRO's best late move—the shrunk brand stops being a trusted benchmark, so the flag triggers reconsideration—was a genuine answer, and CON's "switching regardless of value" gloss overstated it; PRO's visibility asymmetry also outperformed CON's "neutrality" reply. Still, PRO's closing leaned on a somewhat false dilemma and ceded the SKU-scale and cheaper-per-gram points, while CON kept narrowing the debate and left fewer live attacks unanswered. A clear but competitive CON edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A4.1 answer to PRO's dilemma—attention is scarce, not zero, so consolidating the one decision-relevant number and refusing to dilute it with a backward-looking sticker are the same position—defused PRO's strongest pressure, and CON's tracking of "a line of code" becoming SKU-by-SKU "substantially similar" adjudication in B4.1 turned PRO's own answer into evidence for the compliance-burden case.</best_rebuttal>
